# A Two-Grid Finite Element Method for the Nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann Equation Based on a Solution Decomposition

**Abstract**

The nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann equation (PBE) is a widely used implicit-solvent model for the electrostatics of biomolecules in ionic solvent. Its numerical solution is complicated by the point charges, the dielectric jump across the molecular surface, and the exponential nonlinearity. We study a two-grid finite element method for the PBE built on the solution decomposition \(u=G+\Psi+\widehat{\Phi}\) of Xie [J. Comput. Phys. 275 (2014) 294-309], in which _G_ carries the singularities analytically, \(\Psi\) solves a linear interface problem, and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solves a semilinear interface problem for an arbitrary number of ionic species. The nonlinear problem for \(\widehat{\Phi}\) is solved on a coarse mesh only, followed by a single Newton correction on the fine mesh, so that only symmetric positive definite linear systems are solved on the fine mesh. The analysis uses a _C_<sup>2</sup> truncation of the exponential that grows quadratically beyond a level \(\tau\); for \(\tau\) above an explicit bound the truncated problem has the same solution as the original one, and no discrete maximum principle or mesh-angle condition is needed. Under standard piecewise regularity assumptions we prove quasi-optimal energy and _L_<sup>2</sup> estimates and an _L_<sup>4</sup> estimate for the finite element approximation of \(\widehat{\Phi}\), and for the two-grid solution we prove \(|||u-u_h^\text{tg}|||\le C\big(h^{s-1}+H^{2(s-1)+t/2}\big)\) in three dimensions, where \(t=min\{s,\sigma\}-1\). Whenever the dual problem is at least as regular as the primal one (\(\sigma\ge s\)), the coarse mesh can be chosen as _H∼h_<sup>2/5</sup> without loss of accuracy. A manufactured-solution test confirms the predicted rates and the quadratic dependence of the two-grid correction on the coarse error.

**Keywords:** Poisson-Boltzmann equation; solution decomposition; semilinear interface problem; two-grid method; finite element method; a priori error estimates; biomolecular electrostatics.

**MSC 2020:** 65N30, 65N15, 35J61, 92C40.

### 1 Introduction

The Poisson-Boltzmann equation (PBE) is a standard continuum model for the electrostatic potential of a biomolecule in an ionic solvent [32, 14, 4, 26]. It is solved by finite difference and finite element packages such as APBS [5], DelPhi [30] and MIBPB [16], and by boundary integral methods [25, 15]. From the numerical point of view the PBE is an elliptic interface problem with three difficulties: the source is a sum of Dirac distributions at the atomic centers, so the potential is singular there; the dielectric coefficient jumps across the molecular surface; and the ionic charge density depends exponentially on the potential. We refer to the surveys [26] and [34] for the literature on each of these issues.

The point-charge singularities are usually removed by writing the potential as a singular part, known in closed form, plus one or two regular parts that solve interface problems with bounded data \[42, 11, 16, 9, 18\]. In this paper we use the decomposition of Xie \[34\],

\(u=G+\Psi+\widehat{\Phi},\)

where _G_ is the Coulomb potential of the solute charges, \(\Psi\) solves a linear interface problem that carries the boundary and interface conditions, and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solves a semilinear interface problem with homogeneous interface and boundary conditions. The nonlinearity in the problem for \(\widehat{\Phi}\) comes from the ionic charges and acts only in the solvent region. Both \(\Psi\) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solve interface problems with bounded data, and the decomposition allows any number of ionic species. Xie combined it with a finite element method and a modified Newton minimization scheme in a FEniCS-based PBE solver \[34\], and the same splitting has been used in finite element solvers for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations \[35, 8, 41\].

In such solvers most of the work goes into the nonlinear algebraic system for the regular part \(\widehat{\Phi}\). It is usually solved by a damped Newton or Newton-type minimization method \[18, 34\], and every Newton step requires a large linear solve on the fine mesh. The two-grid method of Xu \[36, 37\], see also \[38, 39, 2, 27, 12, 20, 7\], reduces this cost. The nonlinear problem is solved only on a coarse mesh with mesh size _H_, and the solution on the fine mesh with mesh size \(h\checkmark H\) is obtained by one linearized (Newton) correction. The coarse mesh can be much coarser than the fine one, typically \(H\sim h^\gamma\) with \(\gamma<1\), without loss of asymptotic accuracy. Holst, Szypowski and Zhu \[19\] extended the analysis to semilinear interface problems with discontinuous coefficients, with the regularized PBE as their main example, and showed that _H∼h_<sup>2/5</sup> suffices in three dimensions under full regularity. Two-grid methods have also been used to decouple and accelerate finite element solvers for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations \[33, 41\].

Here we apply the two-grid method to Xie’s decomposition and give an a priori error analysis of the resulting scheme. Two points distinguish this setting from \[19\]. First, the nonlinear term in the problem for \(\widehat{\Phi}\) is<tbc>

\(\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi})\chi_{D_s},\rho(\xi)=-\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i\bar{c}_ie^{-Z_i\xi},\)

<tbc>where \(U=G+\Psi\) is the potential of the solute in pure water, _Z<sub>i</sub>_ and \(\bar{c}_i\) are the charge numbers and bulk concentrations of the ionic species, and \(\chi_{D_s}\) is the indicator function of the solvent region. This term depends on _x_ through _U_, vanishes in the solute region, and in the discrete problem _U_ is replaced by the finite element approximation \(U_h=G+\Psi_h\), so the analysis has to account for this perturbation. Second, for nonlinearities of supercritical growth such as the exponential, the analysis in \[19\] relies on a discrete maximum principle, i.e., on a sign condition on the off-diagonal stiffness entries. For tetrahedral meshes generated from molecular surfaces this is a strong restriction. We do not need it. Instead we replace _e<sup>y</sup>_ by a _C_<sup>2</sup> function \(E_\tau(y)\) that equals _e<sup>y</sup>_ for \(y\le\tau\) and is quadratic for \(y>\tau\); this is a smooth version of the overflow safeguard ("blow-up" truncation) used in \[34\]. The truncated nonlinearity is monotone, grows quadratically and has a bounded second derivative. We prove the bound

\(\left\|\widehat{\Phi}\right\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\left\|U\right\|_{L^\infty(D_s)}\)

for the solution of the original problem and conclude that, for every \(\tau\) above an explicit threshold, the truncated problem has the same unique solution. The error analysis can therefore be done for the truncated problem, where no pointwise bounds on discrete solutions are needed, and the results hold for the original problem. As a by-product we obtain a short proof of existence and uniqueness for \(\widehat{\Phi}\) that works in \(H_0^1(\Omega)\) rather than on the set H used in \[34\].

The main results are as follows. Under piecewise _H<sup>s</sup>_ regularity of \(\Psi\) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) and \(H^\sigma\) regularity of a linear dual problem, \(1<s,\sigma\le 2\), we prove that the finite element approximation \(\Phi_h\) of \(\widehat{\Phi}\) computed with the perturbed datum _U<sub>h</sub>_ satisfies energy-norm, _L_<sup>2</sup> and _L_<sup>4</sup> error estimates, in which the perturbation enters only through \(\|\Psi-\Psi_h\|_{L^2(D_s)}\) (Theorems 4.6 and 4.8, Corollary 4.9). For the two-grid solution \(u_h^\mathrm{tg}=G+\Psi_h+\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}\) we prove

\(|||u-u_h^\mathrm{tg}|||\le C\big(h^{s-1}+H^{2(s-1)+t/2}\big),t=\mathrm{min}\{s,\sigma\}-1,\)

in three dimensions (Theorem 5.2), so that the choice \(H\sim h^{(s-1)/(2(s-1)+t/2)}\) keeps the accuracy of the nonlinear fine-mesh solution. If \(\sigma\ge s\), in particular if \(s=\sigma\), this is _H∼h_<sup>2/5</sup>. The estimate holds whether the coarse nonlinear problem uses the fine-mesh datum _U<sub>h</sub>_ or the coarse-mesh datum \(U_H=G+\Psi_H\); with the second choice the whole nonlinear computation stays on the coarse mesh. On the fine mesh the scheme needs only two linear solves with symmetric positive definite matrices, one for \(\Psi_h\) and one for the Newton correction, and both can be done by conjugate gradients with multilevel preconditioners that are robust with respect to the dielectric jump \[40\]. For a symmetric 1:1 electrolyte the truncated nonlinearity is \(\kappa^2\mathrm{sinh}_\tau\), a _C_<sup>2</sup> version of the modified hyperbolic sine of \[34\].

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the dimensionless PBE model, the solution decomposition of \[34\], and the weak formulations. Section 3 introduces the truncated nonlinearity and proves the a priori bounds and the equivalence of the truncated and the original problems. Section 4 contains the finite element discretization and the error estimates for \(\Phi_h\), including the effect of the perturbed datum. Section 5 presents the two-grid algorithm, its error analysis and the choice of the coarse mesh size. Section 6 reports a three-dimensional test with a manufactured solution, and Section 7 contains concluding remarks.

## 2 The Poisson-Boltzmann model and its solution decomposition

### 2.1 The dimensionless PBE model

Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3\) be a bounded Lipschitz domain that is partitioned as \(\overline{\Omega}=\overline{D_p}\cup\overline{D_s}\), where _D<sub>p</sub>_ is the solute region hosting a biomolecule with _n<sub>p</sub>_ atoms, \(D_s=\Omega\backslash\overline{D_p}\) is the solvent region, and \(\Gamma=\partial D_p\) is the interface between them. We assume that \(\overline{D_p}\subset\Omega\), so that \(\Gamma\cap\partial\Omega=\emptyset\), and that both _D<sub>p</sub>_ and _D<sub>s</sub>_ are Lipschitz domains. The _j_th atom has position \(\mathbf{r}_j\in D_p\) and charge number _z<sub>j</sub>_, and the solvent contains _n_ ionic species with charge numbers \(Z_i\neq 0\) and bulk concentrations \(\bar{c}_i\ge 0\) (in mol/L), _i_=1_,...,n_. The two regions are treated as homogeneous dielectric media with relative permittivities \(\epsilon_p\) and \(\epsilon_s\); throughout we only use \(0<\epsilon_p\le\epsilon_s\), and we write \(\epsilon\) for the piecewise constant function with \(\epsilon|_{D_p}=\epsilon_p\) and \(\epsilon|_{D_s}=\epsilon_s\). Following \[34\], when the length is measured in Ångströms and the potential in units of _k<sub>B</sub>T/e<sub>c</sub>_, the PBE model takes the dimensionless form

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
-\epsilon_p\Delta u(\mathbf{r})=\alpha\sum_{j=1}^{n_p}z_j\delta_{\mathbf{r}_j}, & \mathbf{r}\in D_p, \\
-\epsilon_s\Delta u(\mathbf{r})+\rho(u(\mathbf{r}))=0, & \mathbf{r}\in D_s, \\
u(\mathbf{s}^+)=u(\mathbf{s}^-), & \epsilon_s\frac{\partial u(\mathbf{s}^+)}{\partial\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{s})}=\epsilon_p\frac{\partial u(\mathbf{s}^-)}{\partial\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{s})}, & \mathbf{s}\in\Gamma, \\
u(\mathbf{s})=\hat{g}(\mathbf{s}), & \mathbf{s}\in\partial\Omega,
\end{array}\right.\) (1)

where \(\delta_{\mathbf{r}_j}\) is the Dirac distribution at **r**_<sub>j</sub>_, **n** is the unit outward normal of _D<sub>p</sub>_, \(u(\mathbf{s}^\pm)=\mathrm{lim}_{t\rightarrow 0^+}u(\mathbf{s}\pm t\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{s}))\), \(\hat{g}\) is a given boundary function (commonly \(\hat{g}=0\)), and the ionic charge density is described<tbc>

<tbc>by

\(\rho(\xi):=-\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i\bar{c}_ie^{-Z_i\xi},\xi\in\mathbb{R}.\) (2)

The positive constants \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) collect the physical constants; for _T_=298.15 K one has \(\alpha\approx 7042.94\) and \(\beta\approx 4.2413\) \[34\]. We assume throughout that the bulk solution is electrically neutral,<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i\bar{c}_i=0,\bar{c}:=\sum_{i=1}^n\bar{c}_i>0,\) (3)

<tbc>which is the standard physical assumption (the second condition merely excludes the trivial case of pure water) and implies \(\rho(0)=0\). Since

\(\rho'(\xi)=\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i^2\bar{c}_ie^{-Z_i\xi}>0,\) (4)

the function \(\rho\) is strictly increasing. For a symmetric 1:1 electrolyte (_n_=2, _Z_<sub>1</sub>=-_Z_<sub>2</sub>=1, \(\bar{c}_1=\bar{c}_2=I_s\)) we have \(\rho(\xi)=\kappa^2\mathrm{sinh}\xi\) with \(\kappa^2=2\beta I_s\), and the equation in _D<sub>s</sub>_ becomes \(-\epsilon_s\Delta u+\kappa^2\mathrm{sinh}u=0\).

## 2.2 Solution decomposition

To remove the singularities caused by the Dirac distributions, Xie \[34\] decomposes the solution of (1) as<tbc>

\(u=G+\Psi+\widehat{\Phi}\text{in}\Omega,\) (5)

<tbc>where _G_ is the Coulomb potential of the solute charges,<tbc>

\(G(\mathbf{r})=\frac{\alpha}{4\pi\epsilon_p}\sum_{j=1}^{n_p}\frac{z_j}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_j|},\) (6)

<tbc>\(\Psi\) is the solution of the linear interface problem<tbc>

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta\Psi=0 & \text{in}D_p\cup D_s, \\
\Psi(\mathbf{s}^+)=\Psi(\mathbf{s}^-), & \epsilon_s\frac{\partial\Psi(\mathbf{s}^+)}{\partial\mathbf{n}}=\epsilon_p\frac{\partial\Psi(\mathbf{s}^-)}{\partial\mathbf{n}}+(\epsilon_p-\epsilon_s)\frac{\partial G(\mathbf{s})}{\partial\mathbf{n}} & \text{on}\Gamma, \\
\Psi=\hat{g}-G & \text{on}\partial\Omega,
\end{array}\right.\) (7)

<tbc>and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) is the solution of the semilinear interface problem<tbc>

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta\widehat{\Phi}=0 & \text{in}D_p, \\
-\epsilon_s\Delta\widehat{\Phi}+\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi})=0 & \text{in}D_s, \\
\widehat{\Phi}(\mathbf{s}^+)=\widehat{\Phi}(\mathbf{s}^-), & \epsilon_s\frac{\partial\widehat{\Phi}(\mathbf{s}^+)}{\partial\mathbf{n}}=\epsilon_p\frac{\partial\widehat{\Phi}(\mathbf{s}^-)}{\partial\mathbf{n}} & \text{on}\Gamma, \\
\widehat{\Phi}=0 & \text{on}\partial\Omega,
\end{array}\right.\) (8)

<tbc>with

\(U:=G+\Psi.\) (9)

Since \(-\Delta\big(\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_j|}\big)=\delta_{\mathbf{r}_j}\), one checks directly that _u_ defined by (5) satisfies (1); see \[34\]. The functions _G_, \(\Psi\) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) are the contributions of the solute charges, of the boundary and interface<tbc>

conditions, and of the ionic charges, respectively, and \(U=G+\Psi\) is the potential of the solute in pure water. In \[34\] the nonlinearity in (8) is written as \(-\beta\sum_iZ_i\bar{c}_iw_i(\mathbf{r})e^{-Z_i\widehat{\Phi}}\) with _w<sub>i</sub>=e_<sup>-_Z<sub>i</sub>U_</sup>; this is the same as \(\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi})\). Since all atomic centers **r**_<sub>j</sub>_ lie in _D<sub>p</sub>_ and dist(**r**_<sub>j</sub>,<o>D<sub>s</sub></o>)\>_0, the function _G_ is real-analytic in a neighborhood of <o>_D<sub>s</sub>_</o> and, in particular, \(G\in C^\infty(\overline{D_s})\) and \(\nabla G\in L^\infty(D_s)\).

## 2.3 Notation and weak formulations

We use standard notation for Lebesgue and Sobolev spaces. For a measurable set \(D\subseteq\Omega\), \(\left\|\cdot\right\|_{0,p,D}\) denotes the norm of _L<sup>p</sup>(D_), \(1\le p\le\infty\), and \((\cdot,\cdot)_D\) the _L_<sup>2</sup>(_D_) inner product; the subscript _D_ is omitted when \(D=\Omega\). For _s\>_0 we write \(H^s(D_p\cup D_s)\) for the space of functions _v_ with \(v|_{D_p}\in H^s(D_p)\) and \(v|_{D_s}\in H^s(D_s)\), normed by \(\left\|v\right\|_{H^s(D_p\cup D_s)}^2=\left\|v\right\|_{H^s(D_p)}^2+\left\|v\right\|_{H^s(D_s)}^2\). Let \(H_0^1(\Omega)=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):v=0\text{on}\partial\Omega\}\). We shall use the Poincaré and Sobolev inequalities

\(\left\|v\right\|_{0,2}\le C_P\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2},\left\|v\right\|_{0,6}\le C\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2},\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega),\) (10)

and the Gagliardo-Nirenberg (Ladyzhenskaya) inequality in three dimensions \[23\]

\(\left\|v\right\|_{0,4}\le C_L\left\|v\right\|_{0,2}^{1/4}\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2}^{3/4},\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega).\) (11)

By Hölder’s inequality and (10), \(\left\|v\right\|_{0,p}\le C\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2}\) for every \(p\in[1,6]\) and \(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)\).

The bilinear form associated with the dielectric operator is

\(a(v,w):=\epsilon_p\int_{D_p}\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}+\epsilon_s\int_{D_s}\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},v,w\in H^1(\Omega),\) (12)

and we define the energy norm |||_v_|||:=_a(v,v_)<sup>1/2</sup> on \(H_0^1(\Omega)\). Clearly

\(\epsilon_p\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2}^2\le|||v|||^2\le\epsilon_s\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{0,2}^2,a(v,w)\le|||v||||||w|||.\) (13)

Using (10) we have in particular \(\left\|v\right\|_{0,p}\le C|||v|||\) for \(p\in[1,6]\) and \(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)\).

The weak form of (7) reads \[34\]: find \(\Psi\in H^1(\Omega)\) with \(\Psi=\hat{g}-G\) on \(\partial\Omega\) such that

\(a(\Psi,v)=(\epsilon_p-\epsilon_s)\int_{D_s}\nabla G\cdot\nabla v\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega).\) (14)

Here the interface term \((\epsilon_s-\epsilon_p)\int_\Gamma\frac{\partial G}{\partial\mathbf{n}}v\mathrm{d}s\) has been converted into a volume integral by Green’s identity and the harmonicity of _G_ in _D<sub>s</sub>_, which is convenient for complex molecular surfaces. If \(\hat{g}\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)\), problem (14) has a unique solution by the Lax-Milgram lemma \[34, Theorem 4.1\].

The weak form of (8) reads: find \(\widehat{\Phi}\in\mathcal{H}\) such that

\(a(\widehat{\Phi},v)+\big(\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi}),v\big)_{D_s}=0\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega),\) (15)

where

\(\mathcal{H}:=\big\{v\in H_0^1(\Omega):e^{-Z_iv}\in L^2(D_s),i=1,\dots,n\big\}\) (16)

is a subset of \(H_0^1(\Omega)\) on which the nonlinear term is well defined whenever \(U\in L^\infty(D_s)\). It is shown in \[34, Theorem 4.2\] that (15) has a unique solution, which is the unique minimizer of a strictly convex functional on H. In Section 3 we give a different proof that also produces the a priori bound needed for the error analysis.

Throughout the paper we make the following standing assumption on the data.

**Assumption 2.1.** The function \(U=G+\Psi\) defined by (9) satisfies \(U\in L^\infty(D_s)\). We write

\(M_U:=\left\|U\right\|_{0,\infty,D_s}.\) (17)

_Remark_ 2.2. Since \(G\in C^\infty(\overline{D_s})\), Assumption 2.1 only concerns \(\Psi\). If \(\Gamma\) is of class _C_<sup>2</sup>, \(\Omega\) is convex (for instance a box, the usual choice for the PBE) and \(\hat{g}\) is smooth, then \(\Psi\in H^2(D_p)\cap H^2(D_s)\) by \[34, Theorem 4.1\] and the regularity theory of elliptic interface problems \[28, 10\]; because _D<sub>s</sub>_ is a Lipschitz domain in R<sup>3</sup>, the Sobolev embedding \(H^2(D_s)\unknown\rightarrow C(\overline{D_s})\) then gives \(U\in C(\overline{D_s})\). More generally, the assumption holds whenever \(\Psi\in H^s(D_s)\) for some _s\>_3/2; since the regularity Assumption 4.1 below also allows \(1<s\le 3/2\), we keep Assumption 2.1 as a separate standing assumption. The constant _M<sub>U</sub>_ depends only on the linear problem (7), i.e., on the potential of the solute in pure water, and can be estimated before the nonlinear problem is solved.

## 3 A _C_<sup>2</sup> truncation of the nonlinearity and a priori bounds

The exponential growth of \(\rho\) in (2) is the main difficulty in the finite element error analysis of (15): a priori, the Galerkin approximation of \(\widehat{\Phi}\) is only bounded in _H_<sup>1</sup>, and the nonlinearity is neither globally Lipschitz nor of subcritical growth. In \[19\] this is handled by discrete \(L^\infty\) bounds, which require a mesh condition guaranteeing a discrete maximum principle. Here we proceed differently, following the idea of the "blow-up" test in \[34, Algorithm 2\]: the exponential is replaced by a _C_<sup>2</sup> function of quadratic growth, and we show that this does not change the solution.

### 3.1 The truncated exponential

For \(\tau>0\) define

\(E_\tau(y):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
e^y, & y\le\tau, \\
e^\tau\big(1+(y-\tau)+\frac{1}{2}(y-\tau)^2\big), & y>\tau.
\end{array}\right.\) (18)

That is, \(E_\tau\) is the exponential up to the level \(\tau\) and its second-order Taylor polynomial beyond it.

**Lemma 3.1.** _For every_ \(\tau>0\) _the function_ \(E_\tau\) _has the following properties._

(i) \(E_\tau\in C^2(\mathbb{R})\), \(E'_\tau(y)>0\) _and_ \(0<E''_\tau(y)\le e^\tau\) _for all_ \(y\in\mathbb{R}\)_; in particular_ \(E_\tau\) _is strictly increasing and strictly convex._<tbc>

(ii) \(E_\tau(y)=e^y\), \(E'_\tau(y)=e^y\) _and_ \(E''_\tau(y)=e^y\) _for all_ \(y\le\tau\).<tbc>

(iii) _For all_ \(y\in\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\(0<E_\tau(y)\le e^\tau(1+|y|)^2,0<E'_\tau(y)\le e^\tau(1+|y|).\) \(\text{(19)}\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For \(y>\tau\) we have<tbc>

\(E'_\tau(y)=e^\tau\big(1+(y-\tau)\big),E''_\tau(y)=e^\tau,\)

<tbc>while for \(y\le\tau\) all derivatives equal _e<sup>y</sup>_. The one-sided limits of \(E_\tau\), \(E'_\tau\) and \(E''_\tau\) at \(y=\tau\) coincide, which gives (i) and (ii). For (iii), if \(y\le\tau\) then \(E_\tau(y)=e^y\le e^\tau\) and \(E'_\tau(y)\le e^\tau\); if \(y>\tau\) then, since \(0<y-\tau<y\),

\(E_\tau(y)\le e^\tau\big(1+(y-\tau)\big)^2\le e^\tau(1+y)^2,E'_\tau(y)\le e^\tau(1+y).\)

The truncated ionic charge density and its primitive are defined by

\(\rho_\tau(\xi):=-\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i\bar{c}_iE_\tau(-Z_i\xi),P_\tau(\xi):=\int_0^\xi\rho_\tau(\eta)\mathrm{d}\eta,\xi\in\mathbb{R}.\) (20)

Let _Z_<sub>max</sub>:=max_<sub>i</sub>|Z<sub>i</sub>_|.

**Lemma 3.2.** _Let_ (3) _hold and_ \(\tau>0\)_. Then_ \(\rho_\tau\in C^2(\mathbb{R})\) _and the following hold._

(i) \(\rho_\tau(0)=0\) _and_ \(\rho'_\tau(\xi)=\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i^2\bar{c}_iE'_\tau(-Z_i\xi)>0\) _for all_ \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}\)_; hence_ \(\rho_\tau\) _is strictly increasing,_ \(P_\tau\) _is convex and_ \(P_\tau\ge 0\).<tbc>

(ii) _There are constants C_<sub>0</sub>_,C_<sub>1</sub>_,C_<sub>2</sub>_\>_0 _depending only on_ \(\tau,\beta,Z_\mathrm{max}\) _and_ \(\bar{c}\) _such that for all_ \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\(|\rho_\tau(\xi)|\le C_0(1+|\xi|)^2,0<\rho'_\tau(\xi)\le C_1(1+|\xi|),|\rho''_\tau(\xi)|\le C_2,0\le P_\tau(\xi)\le C_0(1+|\xi|)^3.\text{(21)}\)

(iii) \(\rho_\tau(\xi)=\rho(\xi)\), \(\rho'_\tau(\xi)=\rho'(\xi)\) _and_ \(\rho''_\tau(\xi)=\rho''(\xi)\) _whenever_ \(Z_\mathrm{max}|\xi|\le\tau\).<tbc>

<tbc>_Proof._ (i) By (3) and \(E_\tau(0)=1\), \(\rho_\tau(0)=-\beta\sum_iZ_i\bar{c}_i=0\). The formula for \(\rho'_\tau\) follows from the chain rule and \(\rho'_\tau>0\) from Lemma 3.1(i), since \(\bar{c}_i\ge 0\) and \(\bar{c}>0\). Convexity of \(P_\tau\) follows from \(P''_\tau=\rho'_\tau>0\), and \(P_\tau\ge 0\) from \(P_\tau(0)=0\), \(P'_\tau(0)=\rho_\tau(0)=0\) and convexity. (ii) The bounds on \(\rho_\tau\) and \(\rho'_\tau\) follow from (19) and \((1+|Z_i\xi|)\le(1+Z_\mathrm{max})(1+|\xi|)\); for instance<tbc>

\(C_0=\beta e^\tau Z_\mathrm{max}\bar{c}(1+Z_\mathrm{max})^2,C_1=\beta e^\tau Z_\mathrm{max}^2\bar{c}(1+Z_\mathrm{max})\)

<tbc>will do. Since

\(\rho''_\tau(\xi)=-\beta\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i^3\bar{c}_iE''_\tau(-Z_i\xi),\)

Lemma 3.1(i) gives \(|\rho''_\tau(\xi)|\le C_2:=\beta e^\tau Z_\mathrm{max}^3\bar{c}\). The bound on \(P_\tau\) follows by integrating the bound on \(\rho_\tau\). (iii) If \(Z_\mathrm{max}|\xi|\le\tau\) then \(-Z_i\xi\le\tau\) for all _i_, and Lemma 3.1(ii) applies.

_Remark_ 3.3. In the symmetric 1:1 case, \(\rho_\tau(\xi)=\kappa^2\mathrm{sinh}_\tau(\xi)\) and \(\rho'_\tau(\xi)=\kappa^2\mathrm{cosh}_\tau(\xi)\) with

\(\mathrm{sinh}_\tau(\xi):=\frac{1}{2}\big(E_\tau(\xi)-E_\tau(-\xi)\big),\mathrm{cosh}_\tau(\xi):=\frac{1}{2}\big(E'_\tau(\xi)+E'_\tau(-\xi)\big).\) (22)

They are _C_<sup>2</sup> counterparts of the modified hyperbolic functions \(\widetilde{\mathrm{sinh}}\) and \(\widetilde{\mathrm{cosh}}\) of \[34, Eq. (49)\], which are obtained by freezing sinh and cosh at the values \(\pm\mathrm{sinh}\tau\) and \(\mathrm{cosh}\tau\) for \(|\xi|\ge\tau\); those functions are continuous but not differentiable at \(\pm\tau\), and \(\widetilde{\mathrm{cosh}}\) is not the derivative of \(\widetilde{\mathrm{sinh}}\). The functions in (22) coincide with sinh and cosh for \(|\xi|\le\tau\), \(\mathrm{cosh}_\tau=\mathrm{sinh}'_\tau\), and \(\mathrm{sinh}_\tau\) is odd, increasing and of quadratic growth.

## 3.2 The truncated problem and its well-posedness

For \(\tau>0\) consider the truncated version of (15): find \(\Phi_\tau\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) such that<tbc>

\(a(\Phi_\tau,v)+\big(\rho_\tau(U+\Phi_\tau),v\big)_{D_s}=0\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega).\) (23)

<tbc>By Assumption 2.1 and (21), for \(\Phi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) we have \(|\rho_\tau(U+\Phi)|\le C_0(1+M_U+|\Phi|)^2\in L^3(D_s)\) because \(\Phi\in L^6(\Omega)\), so that the nonlinear term in (23) is well defined for every \(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)\subset L^{3/2}(\Omega)\). Let

\(J_\tau(v):=\frac{1}{2}a(v,v)+\int_{D_s}P_\tau(U+v)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},v\in H_0^1(\Omega),\) (24)

which is finite by (21) since \(H_0^1(\Omega)\subset L^3(\Omega)\).

**Theorem 3.4.** _Let Assumption 2.1 and_ (3) _hold and let_ \(\tau>0\)_. Then problem_ (23) _has a unique solution_ \(\Phi_\tau\in H_0^1(\Omega)\)_, which is the unique minimizer of_ \(J_\tau\) _over_ \(H_0^1(\Omega)\)_, and_<tbc>

\(|||\Phi_\tau|||\le\epsilon_p^{-1/2}C_P\left\|\rho_\tau(U)\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\le\epsilon_p^{-1/2}C_PC_0|D_s|^{1/2}(1+M_U)^2.\) (25)

<tbc>_Proof._ The functional \(J_\tau\) is strictly convex on \(H_0^1(\Omega)\), since \(v\mapsto a(v,v)\) is strictly convex and \(P_\tau\) is convex. It is coercive, since \(P_\tau\ge 0\) gives \(J_\tau(v)\ge\frac{1}{2}|||v|||^2\). It is continuous: if \(v_k\rightarrow v\) in \(H_0^1(\Omega)\) then \(v_k\rightarrow v\) in \(L^3(\Omega)\), and since<tbc>

\(0\le P_\tau(U+v)\le C_0\big(1+M_U+|v|\big)^3\text{a.e. in}D_s,\)

<tbc>the Nemytskii operator \(v\mapsto P_\tau(U+v)\) is continuous from _L_<sup>3</sup>(_D<sub>s</sub>_) to _L_<sup>1</sup>(_D<sub>s</sub>_) \[1\]. A continuous convex functional is weakly lower semicontinuous, so \(J_\tau\) has a unique minimizer \(\Phi_\tau\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) \[13, Proposition II.1.2\]. Moreover, \(J_\tau\) is Gâteaux differentiable with

\(J'_\tau(v)w=a(v,w)+\big(\rho_\tau(U+v),w\big)_{D_s},v,w\in H_0^1(\Omega),\)

by dominated convergence, using (21) and \(v,w\in L^6(\Omega)\). Hence the minimizer satisfies (23). Conversely, every solution of (23) is a critical point of the strictly convex functional \(J_\tau\) and therefore its unique minimizer; this proves uniqueness.

For (25), take \(v=\Phi_\tau\) in (23) and subtract \((\rho_\tau(U),\Phi_\tau)_{D_s}\) from both sides:<tbc>

\(|||\Phi_\tau|||^2+\big(\rho_\tau(U+\Phi_\tau)-\rho_\tau(U),\Phi_\tau\big)_{D_s}=-\big(\rho_\tau(U),\Phi_\tau\big)_{D_s}.\)

<tbc>The second term on the left is nonnegative because \(\rho_\tau\) is increasing, so by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, (10) and (13),

\(|||\Phi_\tau|||^2\le\left\|\rho_\tau(U)\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\left\|\Phi_\tau\right\|_{0,2}\le\left\|\rho_\tau(U)\right\|_{0,2,D_s}C_P\epsilon_p^{-1/2}|||\Phi_\tau|||,\)

which gives the first inequality in (25); the second follows from (21), since \(|\rho_\tau(U)|\le C_0(1+M_U)^2\) a.e. in _D<sub>s</sub>_.

## 3.3 A priori \(L^\infty\) bounds and equivalence with the original problem

The following bound is the analogue of \[19, Theorem 2.3\] and \[9, Lemma 3.1\] for the problem (23); its proof uses only the monotonicity of \(\rho_\tau\) and the fact that \(\rho_\tau(0)=0\). No smoothness of \(\Gamma\) beyond the Lipschitz property is required.

**Theorem 3.5.** _Let Assumption 2.1 and_ (3) _hold, let_ \(\tau>0\) _and let_ \(\Phi_\tau\) _be the solution of_ (23)_. Then_

\(-M_U\le\Phi_\tau\le M_U\text{\textit{a.e. in}}\Omega.\) (26)

_The same bound holds for every solution_ \(\widehat{\Phi}\in\mathcal{H}\) _of the original problem_ (15).

_Proof._ Let \(\Phi\) denote either \(\Phi_\tau\) or a solution \(\widehat{\Phi}\in\mathcal{H}\) of (15), and let _r_ denote \(\rho_\tau\) or \(\rho\) accordingly; in both cases _r_ is increasing with _r_(0)=0, and \(r(U+\Phi)\in L^2(D_s)\) (for \(\rho_\tau\) this was shown above; for \(\rho\) it follows from \(U\in L^\infty(D_s)\) and the definition of H). Consider<tbc>

\(\phi:=(\Phi-M_U)^+=max\{\Phi-M_U,0\}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\Phi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) and \(M_U\ge 0\), we have \(\phi\in H_0^1(\Omega)\), \(\phi\ge 0\), and, by \[22, Theorem A.1\] and \[17, Lemma 7.6\],<tbc>

\(\nabla\phi=\nabla\Phi\text{a.e. on}\{\Phi>M_U\},\nabla\phi=0\text{a.e. on}\{\Phi\le M_U\}\)

<tbc>Hence \(a(\Phi,\phi)=a(\phi,\phi)\). On the set \(\{\phi>0\}\cap D_s\) we have \(U+\Phi\ge-M_U+M_U=0\), so \(r(U+\Phi)\ge r(0)=0\) there, and therefore \((r(U+\Phi),\phi)_{D_s}\ge 0\). Taking \(v=\phi\) in the weak formulation gives<tbc>

\(a(\phi,\phi)=a(\Phi,\phi)=-\big(r(U+\Phi),\phi\big)_{D_s}\le 0,\)

<tbc>so that \(|||\phi|||=0\) and \(\phi=0\), i.e., \(\Phi\le M_U\) a.e. For the lower bound, let

\(\psi:=(\Phi+M_U)^-=\mathrm{min}\{\Phi+M_U,0\}\in H_0^1(\Omega),\psi\le 0.\)

As before \(a(\Phi,\psi)=a(\psi,\psi)\), and on \(\{\psi<0\}\cap D_s\) we have \(U+\Phi\le M_U-M_U=0\), so \(r(U+\Phi)\le 0\) and \((r(U+\Phi),\psi)_{D_s}\ge 0\). Taking \(v=\psi\) gives \(a(\psi,\psi)\le 0\), hence \(\psi=0\) and \(\Phi\ge-M_U\) a.e.

We can now state the main result of this section: for a truncation level above an explicit threshold, the truncated problem and the original problem have the same solution.

**Theorem 3.6.** _Let Assumption 2.1 and_ (3) _hold, and let_

\(\tau\ge\tau_0:=2Z_\mathrm{max}M_U.\) (27)

_Then the solution_ \(\Phi_\tau\) _of the truncated problem_ (23) _belongs to_ H _and is the unique solution of the original problem_ (15)_. In particular, the solution_ \(\widehat{\Phi}\) _of_ (15) _does not depend on_ \(\tau\ge\tau_0\)_, satisfies_ \(\left\|\widehat{\Phi}\right\|_{0,\infty}\le M_U\)_, and_<tbc>

\(\left\|U+\widehat{\Phi}\right\|_{0,\infty,D_s}\le 2M_U.\) (28)

<tbc>_Proof._ By Theorem 3.5, \(|\Phi_\tau|\le M_U\) a.e. in \(\Omega\), so that

\(|U+\Phi_\tau|\le 2M_U\text{and}Z_\mathrm{max}|U+\Phi_\tau|\le\tau_0\le\tau\text{a.e. in}D_s.\)

By Lemma 3.2(iii), \(\rho_\tau(U+\Phi_\tau)=\rho(U+\Phi_\tau)\) a.e. in _D<sub>s</sub>_, so \(\Phi_\tau\) satisfies (15); and \(\Phi_\tau\in\mathcal{H}\) because it is bounded. Conversely, let \(\widehat{\Phi}\in\mathcal{H}\) be any solution of (15). By the second part of Theorem 3.5, \(|\widehat{\Phi}|\le M_U\), hence \(\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi})=\rho_\tau(U+\widehat{\Phi})\) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solves (23). By the uniqueness in Theorem 3.4, \(\widehat{\Phi}=\Phi_\tau\).

_Remark_ 3.7. Theorem 3.6 gives a second proof of the existence and uniqueness result \[34, Theorem 4.2\] for \(\widehat{\Phi}\). It also explains why the truncation used in practice is harmless. In \[34\] the exponentials are truncated at \(\tau=85\) to avoid overflow in the first Newton iterations, with the argument that the truncation is inactive near the minimizer; by Theorem 3.6, for every \(\tau\ge 2Z_\mathrm{max}\left\|U\right\|_{0,\infty,D_s}\) the truncated problem coincides with the original one. In the discrete problems below we always use the truncated nonlinearity. A code that uses \(\rho_\tau\) as its overflow safeguard computes exactly this discrete solution, and with the truncation the constants in the error estimates depend on \(\tau\) (through \(e^\tau\)) but not on pointwise bounds of discrete solutions. The smallest constants are obtained for \(\tau\) close to \(\tau_0\), which only requires a bound on the potential of the solute in water in the solvent region; this bound is available once \(\Psi\) has been computed. Since \(|Z_i(U+\widehat{\Phi})|\le\tau_0\) by (28), the factor \(e^{\tau_0}\) reflects the actual size of the ionic densities _e_<sup>-_Z<sub>i</sub>u_</sup> and is not caused by the truncation.

Henceforth we fix \(\tau\ge\tau_0\) and denote by \(\widehat{\Phi}=\Phi_\tau\) the unique solution of (15) and (23). For later use we record the consequences of Theorem 3.6 and Lemma 3.2 that

\(0<c(\mathbf{r}):=\rho'_\tau\big(U(\mathbf{r})+\widehat{\Phi}(\mathbf{r})\big)\le C_1(1+2M_U)=:c_\mathrm{max}\text{for a.e.}\mathbf{r}\in D_s.\) (29)

## 4 Finite element discretization and error estimates

### 4.1 Meshes, spaces and assumptions

From now on, we assume that \(\Omega\) and _D<sub>p</sub>_ are polyhedral, so that the interface \(\Gamma\) is a closed polyhedral surface, and we let {T_<sub>h</sub>_}<sub>_h\>_0</sub> be a family of conforming, shape-regular and quasi-uniform tetrahedral meshes of \(\Omega\) that are fitted to the interface, i.e., every \(T\in\mathcal{T}_h\) satisfies \(T\subset\overline{D_p}\) or \(T\subset\overline{D_s}\). Quasi-uniformity is used only in Section 5, to relate mesh sizes to numbers of unknowns. Here \(h=\mathrm{max}_{T\in\mathcal{T}_h}\mathrm{diam}(T)\), and without loss of generality \(h\le 1\). All constants _C_ below are independent of the mesh, unless stated otherwise. (If \(\Gamma\) is a curved surface, the results below remain valid for meshes that resolve \(\Gamma\) up to _O(h_<sup>2</sup>), cf. \[10, 24, 19\]; we do not pursue this generalization.) Let

\(V_h:=\{v\in C(\overline{\Omega}):v|_T\in\mathbb{P}_1(T)\forall T\in\mathcal{T}_h\}\subset H^1(\Omega),V_h^0:=V_h\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\)

be the spaces of continuous piecewise linear functions. The restriction to piecewise linear elements is for ease of exposition; see Remark 4.11.

**Assumption 4.1** (regularity)**.** There exist \(s,\sigma\in(1,2]\) such that:

(i) the solutions \(\Psi\) of (14) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) of (15) satisfy \(\Psi,\widehat{\Phi}\in H^s(D_p\cup D_s)\);<tbc>

(ii) for every measurable _c_ with \(0\le c\le c_\mathrm{max}\) a.e. in _D<sub>s</sub>_, where _c_<sub>max</sub> is the constant in (29), and every \(f\in L^2(\Omega)\), the solution \(w\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) of the linear dual problem<tbc>

\(a(v,w)+(cv,w)_{D_s}=(f,v)\forall v\in H_0^1(\Omega),\) \(\text{(30)}\)

satisfies \(w\in H^\sigma(D_p\cup D_s)\) and<tbc>

\(\left\|w\right\|_{H^\sigma(D_p\cup D_s)}\le C_R\left\|f\right\|_{0,2},\) \(\text{(31)}\)

with _C<sub>R</sub>_ independent of _c_ and _f_ (it may depend on _c_<sub>max</sub>). (The two cases used below are _c_=0, for the linear component \(\Psi\), and \(c=\rho'_\tau(U+\widehat{\Phi})\), for the nonlinear component \(\widehat{\Phi}\).)

We set

\(t:=\mathrm{min}\{s,\sigma\}-1\in(0,1].\) \(\text{(32)}\)

Both parts of Assumption 4.1 are regularity statements for linear elliptic interface problems with piecewise constant diffusion coefficient: \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solves (8) with the bounded right-hand side \(-\rho(U+\widehat{\Phi})\chi_{D_s}\in L^\infty(\Omega)\) (see (28)), \(\Psi\) solves (7) with data determined by _G_ and \(\hat{g}\), and (30) is an interface problem with a bounded nonnegative reaction coefficient, which can be moved to the right-hand side since \(\left\|cw\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\le c_\mathrm{max}C_P\epsilon_p^{-1/2}\left\|w\right\|\le C\left\|f\right\|_{0,2}\) (test (30) with _v=w_ and use \(c\ge 0\)). Assumptions of this type are common in the analysis of interface problems, see \[24, Assumption 4.3\] and \[19, Eq. (3.11)\].

_Remark_ 4.2. The exponents _s_ and \(\sigma\) are determined by the regularity of the linear interface problems (7) and (30), hence by the geometry of \(\Gamma\) and \(\partial\Omega\) and by the ratio \(\epsilon_s/\epsilon_p\). For the polyhedral interfaces of this section one can in general only expect \(s,\sigma\in(1,2)\), with values depending on the edge and vertex angles of \(\Gamma\) and on \(\epsilon_s/\epsilon_p\) \[21, 28\]. If \(\Gamma\) is of class _C_<sup>2</sup>, \(\Omega\) is convex and \(\hat{g}\) is smooth, then \(s=\sigma=2\) \[28, 10, 34\], because \(G\in C^\infty(\overline{D_s})\) and the right-hand side of (8) is bounded. This case lies outside the polyhedral setting assumed here, but it is the relevant one when \(\Gamma\) is smooth and the mesh approximates it with sufficient accuracy \[24\]. Since \(\Psi\) and \(\widehat{\Phi}\) solve interface problems of the same type with smooth or bounded data, their regularity is limited by the same edge and vertex singularities, and one can usually take \(s=\sigma\). The case \(\sigma<s\) occurs when the solution is smoother than in the worst case, for example for the manufactured solution of Section 6.

**Lemma 4.3.** _For every_ \(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^r(D_p\cup D_s)\) _with_ \(1<r\le 2\) _there exists_ \(v_h\in V_h^0\) _such that_

\(\left\|v-v_h\right\|_{0,2}+h\left\|\left\|v-v_h\right\|\right\|\le C_Ah^r\left\|v\right\|_{H^r(D_p\cup D_s)}.\) (33)

_Proof._ The estimate (33) is a standard consequence of the elementwise interpolation estimates on fitted meshes, i.e., meshes whose elements satisfy \(T\subset\overline{D_p}\) or \(T\subset\overline{D_s}\).

For _r\>_3/2, the nodal interpolant _I<sub>h</sub>v_ is well defined, since _H<sup>r</sup>(D<sub>p</sub>_) and _H<sup>r</sup>(D<sub>s</sub>_) embed into the continuous functions and _v_ is continuous across \(\Gamma\), and the usual elementwise interpolation estimates give (33) because every element lies in <o>_D<sub>p</sub>_</o> or in <o>_D<sub>s</sub>_</o>. For general \(r\in(1,2]\), the nodal interpolant need not be defined, and one instead uses a Scott-Zhang type quasi-interpolant \[31\] whose averaging patches do not cross \(\Gamma\) and which preserves homogeneous boundary values; the local estimates then yield (33) for all \(r\in(1,2]\). We refer to \[10\] and \[24, Theorem 3.5\] for the details.

## 4.2 The linear component

The finite element approximation of \(\Psi\) is defined as in \[34, Algorithm 1\]: find \(\Psi_h\in V_h\) such that \(\Psi_h=I_h^\partial(\hat{g}-G)\) on \(\partial\Omega\) and

\(a(\Psi_h,v)=(\epsilon_p-\epsilon_s)\int_{D_s}\nabla G\cdot\nabla v\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\forall v\in V_h^0,\) (34)

where \(I_h^\partial\) denotes nodal interpolation on the boundary mesh. Since _G_ is smooth near \(\partial\Omega\), the boundary datum \(\hat{g}-G\) is as smooth as \(\hat{g}\). From now on we assume that \(\hat{g}\) is smooth, as is the case in practice (\(\hat{g}=0\) or a smooth far-field approximation), so that nodal interpolation on \(\partial\Omega\) is defined. (If only \(\hat{g}\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)\), \(I_h^\partial\) can be replaced by the trace of a Scott-Zhang quasi-interpolant \[31\].) Problem (34) is a standard discretization of a linear interface problem with piecewise constant coefficients \[3, 10, 29, 24\]. We include a short proof of the error estimate because of the nonhomogeneous Dirichlet datum.

**Lemma 4.4.** _Let Assumption 4.1 hold and let_ \(\hat{g}\) _be smooth. Then for every mesh_ T_<sub>h</sub> of the family, the solutions of_ (14) _and_ (34) _satisfy_

\(\left\|\left\|\Psi-\Psi_h\right\|\right\|\le C_\Psi h^{s-1},\left\|\Psi-\Psi_h\right\|_{0,2}\le C_\Psi h^{s+\sigma-2}\le C_\Psi h^{s-1+t},\) (35)

_with_ \(s,\sigma\) _and t as in Assumption 4.1 and_ \(C_\Psi\) _independent of h._

_Proof._ Since \(\hat{g}-G\) is smooth on \(\partial\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\cap\partial\Omega=\emptyset\), there is a lifting \(\bar{\Psi}\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega})\) with \(\bar{\Psi}=\hat{g}-G\) on \(\partial\Omega\) and \(\bar{\Psi}=0\) in a neighborhood of \(\Gamma\). Then \(I_h\bar{\Psi}\in V_h\) has the boundary values \(I_h^\partial(\hat{g}-G)\), so that \(\Psi_h-I_h\bar{\Psi}\in V_h^0\), and

\(\left\|\left\|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right\|\right\|+h^{-1}\left\|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right\|_{0,2}+h^{-1}\left\|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right\|_{0,2,\partial\Omega}\le C_\bar{\Psi}h\) (36)

by the standard interpolation estimates in \(\Omega\) and on the faces of \(\partial\Omega\), with \(C_\bar{\Psi}\) depending on the _C_<sup>2</sup> norm of \(\bar{\Psi}\). Moreover \(\Psi-\bar{\Psi}\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^s(D_p\cup D_s)\) by Assumption 4.1(i). Subtracting (34) from (14) gives the Galerkin orthogonality

\(a(\Psi-\Psi_h,v)=0\forall v\in V_h^0.\) (37)

_Energy estimate._ Let \(v_h\in V_h^0\) be the approximation of \(\Psi-\bar{\Psi}\) provided by Lemma 4.3 with _r=s_, and set \(\chi_h:=I_h\bar{\Psi}+v_h\in V_h\); then \(\chi_h-\Psi_h\in V_h^0\), so by (37)<tbc>

\(\left\|\left\|\Psi-\Psi_h\right\|\right\|^2=a(\Psi-\Psi_h,\Psi-\chi_h)\le\left\|\left\|\Psi-\Psi_h\right\|\right\|\left\|\Psi-\chi_h\right\|,\)

<tbc>and by (36) and (33),

\(\left|\left|\Psi-\chi_h\right|\right|\le\left|\left|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|+\left|\left|\Psi-\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|-v_h\right|\right|\le C_\bar{\Psi}h+C_Ah^{s-1}\left|\left|\Psi-\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|_{H^s(D_p\cup D_s)}\le Ch^{s-1}.\)

_L_<sup>2</sup> _estimate._ Write \(e:=\Psi-\Psi_h=(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi})+e^0\) with \(e^0:=(\Psi-\bar{\Psi})-(\Psi_h-I_h\bar{\Psi})\in H_0^1(\Omega)\). By (36), \(\left|\left|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|_{0,2}\le Ch^2\), so it suffices to bound \(\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\). Let \(w\in H_0^1(\Omega)\) solve the dual problem (30) with _c_=0 and _f=e_<sup>0</sup>, and let \(w_h\in V_h^0\) be its Galerkin approximation, so that \(\left|\left|\left|w-w_h\right|\right|\right|\le Ch^{\sigma-1}\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\) by Lemma 4.3 and Assumption 4.1(ii). Using (37) in the form \(a(e^0,w_h)=a(e,w_h)-a(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},w_h)=-a(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},w_h)\), we obtain<tbc>

\(\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}^2=a(e^0,w)=a(e^0,w-w_h)-a(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},w_h-w)-a(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},w).\) (38)

<tbc>The first two terms are bounded by \(C\big(\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|+\left|\left|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|\right)\left|\left|\left|\Psi w-w_h\right|\right|\right|\le Ch^{s-1}h^{\sigma-1}\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\), where \(\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|\le\left|\left|\left|\Psi e\right|\right|+\left|\left|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|\le Ch^{s-1}\) by the energy estimate. For the last term we integrate by parts in _D<sub>p</sub>_ and _D<sub>s</sub>_: since \(-\nabla\cdot(\epsilon\nabla w)=e^0\) in \(D_p\cup D_s\) and the flux \(\epsilon\partial w/\partial\mathbf{n}\) is continuous across \(\Gamma\), while \(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\) vanishes near \(\Gamma\),

\(a(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},w)=\big(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi},e^0\big)+\epsilon_s\int_{\partial\Omega}(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi})\frac{\partial w}{\partial\mathbf{n}}\mathrm{d}s.\)

The volume term is bounded by \(Ch^2\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\) by (36). For the boundary term, if \(\sigma>3/2\) the trace \(\partial w/\partial\mathbf{n}\in L^2(\partial\Omega)\) satisfies \(\left|\left|\left|\partial w/\partial\mathbf{n}\right|\right|\right|_{0,2,\partial\Omega}\le C\left|\left|\left|w\right|\right|\right|_{H^\sigma(D_s)}\le C\left|\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\), and (36) bounds the term by \(Ch^2\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\). If \(1<\sigma\le 3/2\), the conormal derivative is defined by Green’s formula as an element of \(H^{\sigma-3/2}(\partial\Omega)\) with norm bounded by \(C\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\), and interpolating the \(L^2(\partial\Omega)\) and \(H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)\) interpolation estimates for \(\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\) on the faces of \(\partial\Omega\) gives \(\left|\left|\left|\bar{\Psi}-I_h\bar{\Psi}\right|\right|\right|_{H^{3/2-\sigma}(\partial\Omega)}\le Ch^{\sigma+1/2}\), so that the term is bounded by \(Ch^{\sigma+1/2}\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\). Since \(s+\sigma-2\le\mathrm{min}\{\sigma+1/2,2\}\) for \(s,\sigma\in(1,2]\), all contributions in (38) are bounded by \(Ch^{s+\sigma-2}\left|\left|\left|e^0\right|\right|\right|_{0,2}\), which proves the _L_<sup>2</sup> estimate; the last inequality in (35) uses \(h\le 1\) and \(\sigma-1\ge t\).

Since \(h\le 1\) and \(s,\sigma>1\), Lemma 4.4 and (13) give, for every mesh of the family,

\(\left|\left|\Psi_h\right|\right|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\left|\left|\Psi\right|\right|_{H^1(\Omega)}+\left|\left|\Psi-\Psi_h\right|\right|_{0,2}+\epsilon_p^{-1/2}\left|\left|\left|\Psi-\Psi_h\right|\right|\right|\le\left|\left|\Psi\right|\right|_{H^1(\Omega)}+\big(1+\epsilon_p^{-1/2}\big)C_\Psi=:\Lambda.\) (39)

The constant \(\Lambda\) does not depend on the mesh; in Section 5 it is used for both the fine mesh T_<sub>h</sub>_ and the coarse mesh T_<sub>H</sub>_. We set \(U_h:=G+\Psi_h\).

## 4.3 The nonlinear component: discrete problem and stability

In the discrete problem for \(\widehat{\Phi}\), the function _U_ is not available and is replaced by an approximation. To treat the fine and coarse meshes of the two-grid method simultaneously, we consider a generic mesh T_<sub>h</sub>_ and a generic datum<tbc>

\(U^*:=G+\Psi^*,\Psi^*\in H^1(\Omega),\left|\left|\Psi^*\right|\right|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\Lambda,\) (40)

<tbc>where \(\Lambda>0\) is a fixed constant. With \(\Lambda\) as in (39), both \(\Psi^*=\Psi_h\) and \(\Psi^*=\Psi_H\) are admissible. The discrete nonlinear problem reads: find \(\Phi_h\in V_h^0\) such that<tbc>

\(a(\Phi_h,v)+\big(\rho_\tau(U^*+\Phi_h),v\big)_{D_s}=0\forall v\in V_h^0;\) (41)

its well-posedness is established in Lemma 4.5 below. We write

\(\delta:=\left\|\Psi-\Psi^*\right\|_{0,2,D_s}=\left\|U-U^*\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\) (42)

for the size of the data perturbation. The nonlinearity in (41) is the truncated one, in accordance with Remark 3.7, and that \(U^*+\Phi_h\) need not be bounded pointwise.

**Lemma 4.5.** _Let Assumption 2.1 and_ (3) _hold,_ \(\tau>0\)_, and let U_<sup>∗</sup> _be as in_ (40)_. Then_ (41) _has a unique solution_ \(\Phi_h\in V_h^0\)_, and_

\(\left\|\Phi_h\right\|\le\epsilon_p^{-1/2}C_P\left\|\rho_\tau(U^*)\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\le C_\Lambda,\) (43)

_where_ \(C_\Lambda\) _depends only on_ \(\tau,\beta,Z_i,\bar{c}_i,\epsilon_p,\Omega\), \(\left\|G\right\|_{H^1(D_s)}\) _and_ \(\Lambda\)_, but not on h._

_Proof._ The functional<tbc>

\(J_\tau^*(v):=\frac{1}{2}a(v,v)+\int_{D_s}P_\tau(U^*+v)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},v\in V_h^0,\)

<tbc>is well defined on \(V_h^0\) because \(U^*\in L^6(D_s)\) (recall that \(G\in C^\infty(\overline{D_s})\) and \(\Psi^*\in H^1(\Omega)\unknown\rightarrow L^6(\Omega)\)) and \(v\in L^6(\Omega)\), and the argument of Theorem 3.4 carries over to the finite-dimensional space \(V_h^0\): \(J_\tau^*\) is strictly convex, continuous and coercive, so it has a unique minimizer, which is the unique solution of (41). The first inequality in (43) is proved exactly as (25). For the second, (21) gives<tbc>

\(\left\|\rho_\tau(U^*)\right\|_{0,2,D_s}\le C_0\left\|(1+|U^*|)^2\right\|_{0,2,D_s}=C_0\left\|1+|U^*|\right\|_{0,4,D_s}^2\le C_0\big(|D_s|^{1/4}+\left\|U^*\right\|_{0,4,D_s}\big)^2,\)

<tbc>and

\(\left\|U^*\right\|_{0,4,D_s}\le C\left\|U^*\right\|_{H^1(D_s)}\le C\big(\left\|G\right\|_{H^1(D_s)}+\Lambda\big)\)

by the Sobolev embedding on the Lipschitz domain _D<sub>s</sub>_.

We shall repeatedly use the following elementary consequence of the mean value theorem and Lemma 3.2(ii): for all \(\xi_1,\xi_2\in\mathbb{R}\),

\(|\rho_\tau(\xi_1)-\rho_\tau(\xi_2)|\le C_1\big(1+|\xi_1|+|\xi_1-\xi_2|\big)|\xi_1-\xi_2|,\) (44)

which follows from \(\rho_\tau(\xi_1)-\rho_\tau(\xi_2)=\rho'_\tau(\zeta)(\xi_1-\xi_2)\) with \(\zeta\) between \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\), so that \(|\zeta|\le|\xi_1|+|\xi_1-\xi_2|\).

## 5 The two-grid algorithm and its analysis

### 5.1 The algorithm

Let T_<sub>H</sub>_ be a coarse mesh with mesh size _H_ from the family introduced in Section 4, and let T_<sub>h</sub>_, _h\<H_, be obtained from T_<sub>H</sub>_ by (possibly repeated) uniform refinement that keeps it in the family (e.g., red refinement of tetrahedra), so that T_<sub>h</sub>_ is fitted to \(\Gamma\) and the finite element spaces are nested, \(V_H^0\subset V_h^0\). The two-grid solution decomposition scheme is described in Algorithm 1. In Step 3 the datum \(\Psi^\sharp\) used to assemble the coarse nonlinear problem may be either the fine-mesh approximation \(\Psi_h\) or a coarse-mesh approximation \(\Psi_H\in V_H\) defined by (34) on T_<sub>H</sub>_; both choices are covered by the analysis below (see Remark 5.5 for a discussion).

**Algorithm 1** Two-grid PBE solution decomposition scheme

**Require:** atomic positions **r**_<sub>j</sub>_ and charges _z<sub>j</sub>_; ionic species \((Z_i,\bar{c}_i)\); permittivities \(\epsilon_p,\epsilon_s\); boundary value \(\hat{g}\); truncation level \(\tau\); meshes T_<sub>H</sub>_, T_<sub>h</sub>_.

1: Compute _G_ and \(\nabla G\) from (6).

2: **(Fine linear solve.)** Find \(\Psi_h\in V_h\) with \(\Psi_h=I_h^\partial(\hat{g}-G)\) on \(\partial\Omega\) satisfying (34); set \(U_h:=G+\Psi_h\). Choose \(\Psi^\sharp\in\{\Psi_h,\Psi_H\}\), where \(\Psi_H\in V_H\) is computed by (34) on T_<sub>H</sub>_ if this variant is chosen, and set \(U^\sharp:=G+\Psi^\sharp\).

3: **(Coarse nonlinear solve.)** Find \(\Phi_H\in V_H^0\) such that

\(a(\Phi_H,v)+\left(\rho_\tau(U^\sharp+\Phi_H),v\right)_{D_s}=0\forall v\in V_H^0.\) (57)

4: **(Fine linear solve: one Newton correction.)** Find \(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}\in V_h^0\) such that for all \(v\in V_h^0\)

\(a(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg},v)+\left(\rho'_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H)\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg},v\right)_{D_s}=\left(\rho'_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H)\Phi_H-\rho_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H),v\right)_{D_s}.\) (58)

**Ensure:** \(u_h^\mathrm{tg}:=G+\Psi_h+\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}\).

The coarse problem (57) is problem (41) on T_<sub>H</sub>_ with datum \(\Psi^*=\Psi^\sharp\). It has a unique solution by Lemma 4.5 and can be solved, for example, by the modified Newton minimization scheme of \[34, Algorithm 2\]; for the truncated nonlinearity this is a descent method for the strictly convex functional \(J_\tau^*\) of Lemma 4.5 with \(U^*=U^\sharp\) and, with a suitable line search, converges from any initial guess. Writing \(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}=\Phi_H+d_h\), the fine problem (58) is equivalent to the Newton correction equation

\(a(d_h,v)+\left(\rho'_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H)d_h,v\right)_{D_s}=-\left[a(\Phi_H,v)+\left(\rho_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H),v\right)_{D_s}\right]\forall v\in V_h^0,\) (59)

whose right-hand side is the residual of the coarse solution in the fine problem (41) with _U_<sup>∗</sup>=_U<sub>h</sub>_. The bilinear form \(B_h(v,w):=a(v,w)+(\rho'_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H)v,w)_{D_s}\) on the left of (59) is symmetric and, since \(\rho'_\tau>0\), it satisfies

\(|||v|||^2\le B_h(v,v)\le\left(1+C_1\epsilon_p^{-1}C_P^2\big(1+\|U_h+\Phi_H\|_{0,\infty,D_s}\big)\right)|||v|||^2\forall v\in V_h^0,\) (60)

where the upper bound uses (21) and the fact that \(U_h+\Phi_H\) is bounded on _D<sub>s</sub>_ (_G_ is smooth on <o>_D<sub>s</sub>_</o> and \(\Psi_h+\Phi_H\) is piecewise linear). Thus only two symmetric positive definite systems are solved on the fine mesh, one for \(\Psi_h\) and one for _d<sub>h</sub>_, and both can be solved by preconditioned conjugate gradients with multilevel preconditioners that are robust with respect to the jump of \(\epsilon\) \[40\]. The coefficient \(\rho'_\tau(U_h+\Phi_H)\) in (58) is bounded on each element but may be large where the truncation<tbc>

is active; the analysis does not use an upper bound for it. Since \(\Phi_H\in V_h^0\), Step 4 is one Newton step on the fine mesh started from the coarse solution, cf. \[37, 19\].

## 5.2 Error analysis

Throughout this subsection, \(\Phi_h\in V_h^0\) denotes the solution of the fine-mesh nonlinear problem (41) with _U_<sup>∗</sup>=_U<sub>h</sub>_, i.e., the "exact" fine-mesh finite element solution, and \(u_h=G+\Psi_h+\Phi_h\) as in Corollary 4.10. The first lemma is the analogue of \[19, Lemma 4.1\] and shows that the two-grid solution differs from the fine-mesh solution by a quantity that is quadratic in the coarse-mesh error.

**Lemma 5.1.** _Let Assumption 2.1 and_ (3) _hold and_ \(\tau>0\)_. Let_ \(\Phi_H\in V_H^0\subset V_h^0\) _be any function and let_ \(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}\in V_h^0\) _be defined by_ (58)_. Then_

\(\left|\left|\Phi_h-\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}\right|\right|\right|\le\frac{1}{2}C_2C_P\epsilon_p^{-1/2}\left|\left|\Phi_h-\Phi_H\right|\right|_{0,4}^2.\) (61)

_Proof._ Write \(b(\xi):=\rho_\tau(U_h+\xi)\) for the fine-mesh nonlinearity, so that \(b'(\xi)=\rho'_\tau(U_h+\xi)\) and \(|b''(\xi)|\le C_2\) a.e. in _D<sub>s</sub>_ by (21). Let \(\chi\in V_h^0\) and put \(\theta:=\Phi_h-\Phi_H\in V_h^0\). By Taylor’s formula with integral remainder, a.e. in _D<sub>s</sub>_,<tbc>

\(b(\Phi_h)=b(\Phi_H)+b'(\Phi_H)\theta+\int_0^1(1-\vartheta)b''(\Phi_H+\vartheta\theta)\theta^2\mathrm{d}\vartheta.\)

<tbc>Testing the fine problem (41) (with _U_<sup>∗</sup>=_U<sub>h</sub>_) with \(\chi\) and inserting this expansion,

\(0=a(\Phi_h,\chi)+\left(b(\Phi_h),\chi\right)_{D_s}=a(\Phi_H,\chi)+\left(b(\Phi_H),\chi\right)_{D_s}+a(\theta,\chi)+\left(b'(\Phi_H)\theta,\chi\right)_{D_s}+R(\chi),\text{(62)}\)

where

\(R(\chi):=\int_0^1(1-\vartheta)\left(b''(\Phi_H+\vartheta\theta)\theta^2,\chi\right)_{D_s}\mathrm{d}\vartheta\)

satisfies

\(|R(\chi)|\le\frac{1}{2}C_2\left|\left|\theta\right|\right|_{0,4}^2\left|\left|\chi\right|\right|_{0,2}.\) (63)

On the other hand, (58) can be written as<tbc>

\(a(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}-\Phi_H,\chi)+\left(b'(\Phi_H)(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}-\Phi_H),\chi\right)_{D_s}=-a(\Phi_H,\chi)-\left(b(\Phi_H),\chi\right)_{D_s}.\)

<tbc>Adding this identity to (62) and rearranging gives, with \(\omega:=\Phi_h-\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}=\theta-(\Phi_h^\mathrm{tg}-\Phi_H)\),<tbc>

\(a(\omega,\chi)+\left(b'(\Phi_H)\omega,\chi\right)_{D_s}=-R(\chi)\forall\chi\in V_h^0.\)

<tbc>Choosing \(\chi=\omega\), using \(b'>0\), (63), (10) and (13),

\(\left|\left|\left|\omega\right|\right|\right|^2\le a(\omega,\omega)+\left(b'(\Phi_H)\omega,\omega\right)_{D_s}=-R(\omega)\le\frac{1}{2}C_2\left|\left|\theta\right|\right|_{0,4}^2C_P\epsilon_p^{-1/2}\left|\left|\left|\omega\right|\right|\right|,\)

which gives (61) after dividing by \(\left|\left|\left|\omega\right|\right|\right|\).

We now combine Lemma 5.1 with the _L_<sup>4</sup> estimates of Corollary 4.9, applied on both meshes.

## 6.1 Setting

Let \(\Omega=(-1,1)^3\), \(D_p=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})^3\), \(\epsilon_p=2\), \(\epsilon_s=80\), and consider a symmetric 1:1 electrolyte with \(\kappa^2=40\) in _D<sub>s</sub>_. We solve<tbc>

\(-\nabla\cdot(\epsilon\nabla\Phi)+\kappa^2\chi_{D_s}sinh(U+\Phi)=f\text{in}\Omega,\Phi=0\text{on}\partial\Omega,\) (69)

<tbc>with the homogeneous interface conditions of (8), where the source _f_ is chosen so that the exact solution (denoted by \(\Phi\) in this section) is

\(\Phi(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{4}q(x)q(y)q(z),q(x)=cos(2\pi x)-1,\)

and the datum is \(U(x,y,z)=2cos(\pi x)cos(\pi y)cos(\pi z)\), so that _M<sub>U</sub>_=2. The domain is partitioned into _N_<sup>3</sup> cubes of side _h_=2_/N_, each split into six Kuhn tetrahedra (we identify _h_ with the cube side, which is proportional to the element diameter); for _N_ divisible by 4 the mesh is fitted to \(\Gamma\), and the meshes for _N_ and 2_N_ are nested, so that \(V_H^0\subset V_h^0\) and the prolongation of \(\Phi_H\) to the fine mesh in Step 4 of Algorithm 1 is exact. ## 7 Concluding remarks

We have analyzed a two-grid finite element method for the nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann equation based on the solution decomposition \(u=G+\Psi+\widehat{\Phi}\) of \[34\]. The nonlinear problem for \(\widehat{\Phi}\) is solved only on a coarse mesh, and the fine-mesh approximation is obtained by one Newton correction, so that only two symmetric positive definite linear systems are solved on the fine mesh. The analysis uses a _C_<sup>2</sup> truncation of the exponential that grows quadratically above a level \(\tau\). For \(\tau\ge 2Z_\mathrm{max}\left\|G+\Psi\right\|_{L^\infty(D_s)}\) the truncated problem has the same solution as the original one; this gives a new proof of well-posedness, shows that the overflow safeguard used in practice does not change the solution, and leads to error estimates that need no discrete maximum principle and no angle condition on the meshes. Under piecewise _H<sup>s</sup>_ regularity of the primal problem and \(H^\sigma\) regularity of a linear dual problem we proved \(\left\|\text{\textit{\textbf{}}}u-u_h^\mathrm{tg}\right\|\le C(h^{s-1}+H^{2(s-1)+t/2})\) with \(t=\mathrm{min}\{s,\sigma\}-1\), so that _H∼h_<sup>2/5</sup> suffices whenever \(\sigma\ge s\). The estimates include the error from replacing \(U=G+\Psi\) by its finite element approximation, allow the coarse problem to be assembled with coarse-mesh data, and hold for any number of ionic species. A test with a manufactured solution in three dimensions agrees with these results.

Several extensions seem possible. Higher-order elements, and meshes that only approximate a curved interface, could be treated by combining the arguments of Section 4 with the approximation results of \[24\]. The same approach should apply to other regularized forms of the PBE, such as the two-component splitting of \[9, 18\]. For the size-modified PBE, whose nonlinearity is bounded, no truncation would be needed. The combination of solution decomposition and two-grid linearization can also be used for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations of ion channels \[35, 8\], where the coupling between potential and concentrations takes the place of the exponential nonlinearity; we plan to study this in future work, together with experiments on proteins using the PBE finite element package of \[34\].
